analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical makers to prove their products are safe before they can be sold.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 12 House Democrats, never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled the nation's main toxics law. For the first time, chemical manufacturers — not just pesticide and drug makers — would have to certify, over the CEO's signature, that each chemical they sell meets a health safety standard, or admit there is not enough data to say so. The EPA would have to review at least 300 of the most worrisome chemicals first, ban or restrict any chemical that fails the standard, test for chemicals in human blood and cord blood, and post all safety data on a public database. The goal was to eliminate children's, workers', and consumers' exposure to harmful chemicals by 2020.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, workers who handle chemicals, and everyday consumers. Today, most chemicals on the market have never had a federal safety review: the bill's own findings state the EPA had reviewed the health risks of only about 2 percent of the 62,000 chemicals in use when the current law passed in 1976, and had banned or restricted only 5 substances in 29 years. The bill would shift the burden of proof onto manufacturers and give the public access to all the safety data.

how_it_helps.text: Each manufacturer must submit, signed by its chief executive, a certification that each chemical meets a safety standard protecting fetuses, infants, children, and workers — or state that the data are insufficient — and update that information at least every three years.

The EPA must list a priority list of at least 300 chemicals for safety determinations within 18 months, adding at least 200 per year, and any new chemical would be barred from the market 90 days after enactment unless the EPA finds it meets the safety standard.

A chemical that fails the safety standard — or whose manufacturer fails to comply — could no longer be manufactured, imported, or sold, and the EPA could bar specific uses in consumer products that expose people at home beyond the standard.

The CDC would run biomonitoring studies, at manufacturers' expense, to find industrial chemicals in human blood, tissue, and cord blood; a priority chemical found in cord blood would be presumed to have failed the safety standard unless the manufacturer proves otherwise.
All toxicity, use, and exposure data would go into an Internet-accessible public database, and the bill guarantees states can keep stricter rules of their own.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers bear the cost: gathering and submitting toxicity data for every chemical they sell, paying for nationwide biomonitoring through user fees, CEO certification liability, and the risk of losing markets for any chemical that cannot be shown safe. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to prices, and products made with chemicals that fail could be reformulated or disappear.

drawbacks.text: The testing and data requirements would be costly, and smaller manufacturers would bear a disproportionate burden even though the bill sets up green chemistry centers to help them.

The bill uses hard deadlines with automatic consequences: if the EPA itself misses its five-year deadline on a priority chemical, that chemical can no longer be sold — so agency delays, not just company conduct, could disrupt product supply.
Banning or restricting chemicals that fail the standard could force reformulation or removal of products consumers rely on, and compliance costs would likely flow into prices for everyday goods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large: tens of thousands of chemicals sold with essentially no federal safety review would finally have to be tested, and the most dangerous ones could be banned. The real costs fall on manufacturers, with some pass-through to consumers, and the bill's rigid deadlines — where EPA delay itself triggers a market ban — are a design flaw an honest supporter would acknowledge. On balance it is a strong health-protection bill with real but manageable compliance costs, and it preserves states' ability to go further.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, which never considered it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Hilda Solis, joined by Rep. Henry Waxman, introduced the Kid-Safe Chemicals Act of 2008 on May 20, 2008 to overhaul the Toxic Substances Control Act.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on May 20, 2008, and referred again to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials the next day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; that subcommittee referral was the bill's last action of record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

The bill's own findings describe the status quo it would have changed: the EPA had reviewed the health risks of only about 2 percent of the 62,000 chemicals in use in 1976 and had banned or restricted only 5 substances in the 29 years since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they continue to sell tens of thousands of chemicals without any requirement to prove they are safe, and the EPA continues to operate under the same law under which it restricted only 5 substances in nearly three decades. Consumers and families are left with the pre-2008 status quo, including chemicals detected in cord blood with no federal safety determination.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers, on the status quo

for.name: Rep. Hilda Solis
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Kid-Safe Chemicals Act of 2008 to require chemical makers to prove safety before sale.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill as an original co-sponsor.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (John Dingell, D-MI)
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule consideration
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's referral to the environment subcommittee was its last action of record.

against.name: Chemical manufacturers (led by the American Chemistry Council)
against.role: Industry representing companies that make and sell the chemicals covered by the bill
against.what_they_did: Opposed a TSCA overhaul that would have required pre-market safety proof for their products.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 11 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill would force them to prove every chemical they sell meets a child-protective safety standard, pay for biomonitoring, and lose markets for chemicals that fail — ending a system in which most chemicals sell with no pre-market safety review at all. Their interest in the status quo runs against the public's interest in tested products.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers that use industrial chemicals
industries.note: They would face reformulation costs and possible loss of ingredients, but would also gain certainty and access to a public toxicity database; their exposure risk at home is exactly what the bill targets.
The bill creates expedited review, marketing designations, awards, and regional research centers to promote safer substitutes — new markets for companies making safer chemicals.
Mandatory data submission, minimum testing requirements, and manufacturer-funded CDC biomonitoring studies would generate a large stream of paid testing work.
